Chernihiv Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Chernihiv, Ukraine

Not demolished. Chernihiv's Jewish history may extend to Khazar-era Jewish settlement as early as the 11th century, with a documented community from the 13th; Jews returned in the early 17th century, though this community was destroyed during the 1648 Khmelnytsky Uprising. A synagogue was built in 1864; by 1897, 8,805 Jews (29%, of 27,006 total) lived there, primarily in trade and commerce. Chabad rabbi Perez Hen and his son Hayyim David Zevi Hen led religious life through the mid-late 19th century, when four synagogues operated. The community survived multiple pogroms - one in 1905 (one killed, many wounded, grave still on-site) and a larger Denikin-Petliura pogrom (40 killed, 100 wounded, 30 houses destroyed) during the Russian Civil War. Population reached 12,204 (17.79%) by 1939. German occupation (September 1941-September 1943) began with 19 Jews shot by the Sonderkommando that September, followed by 260 more shot October 23-24; only 57 remained alive by December 1941, all later killed. Victims from surrounding districts, Hungary, and Romania were also murdered here, with total Holocaust deaths estimated around 2,000. A postwar community of 219 registered in 1946, though its last synagogue closed during 1959's anti-religious campaign; reestablished in 1989 alongside a Jewish Culture Center, the community numbered 4,558 by the 1989 census and around 3,500 by 2001, now including a kindergarten, Sunday school, synagogue, and choir under Rabbi Israel Silberstein. This cemetery, appearing on 1880s Russian maps with tombstones confirming late-19th-century origins, has separate men's and women's sections; the oldest preserved gravestone (February 1903) belongs to Benjamin Isaakovich Mindelis. The last known Chabad Hasidic burial occurred in 1975, when the cemetery formally closed; German troops partially destroyed the site during occupation.
